about: Industrierobotik (IRB, robot kinematics), FH Technikum Wien master's programme, winter term 2020, after the lecture slides of Ajanović (2020), based on slides by M. Aburaia, chapters 01–05, and the ABB IRB 120 product specification 3HAC035960-001, revision U (ABB 2020). Pages are the PDF pages of each file, read in their text layer and, where the formulas had no text, from the page images, on 2 Nov 2026; the slide numbers printed on the slides run one to three ahead of the PDF pages. The slides have worked examples but no separate exercise sheet; their printed results are used where they exist (ch. 1, pp. 38–39; ch. 2, pp. 16, 34, 35, 38, 46, 48, 52; ch. 3, pp. 3, 26; ch. 5, pp. 8, 10, 19, 20; ABB p. 31); the rest were worked by hand from the slides' equations and say so. tests/unit/labs-data.test.js recomputes every answer with the core and fails if they disagree.

labs.title: How many drives? Grübler's count
labs.idea: Count the links and joints of a robot and the count says how many drives set its pose: each free body has three freedoms in the plane, six in space, and each joint takes away all but its own.

equations.eq: DOF = T(n − 1) − Σ (T − fi)
equations.note: Freedoms of the n − 1 moving links less the constraints of the g joints; n counts the base

equations.eq: DOF = T(n − 1 − g) + Σ fi
equations.note: Grübler's formula; T = 3 for plane or spherical mechanisms, 6 for spatial ones

equations.eq: f = 1 turning or sliding, 2 cylindrical or universal, 3 ball joint
equations.note: The freedoms of the common joints

practice.question: A 3R arm in the plane: T = 3, n = 4 links with the base, g = 3 turning joints. How many degrees of freedom?
A four-bar linkage: T = 3, n = 4, g = 4 turning joints. Its degrees of freedom?
The ABB IRB 120: six turning axes in a row in space, base and six moving links. Its degrees of freedom?
practice.source: Worked by hand from ch. 1, p. 37, with the six axes of ABB (2020), p. 32

labs.title: One point, two frames: the homogeneous transform
labs.idea: A point has different coordinates in a frame that is turned and moved. One 3 × 3 matrix holds the turn and the move together, and its inverse brings the point back.

equations.eq: Rp = Gp + r
equations.note: A frame moved by r: the coordinates add

equations.eq: R(θ) = [cos θ −sin θ; sin θ cos θ]
equations.note: The plane rotation; orthonormal, so its transpose is its inverse and R(θ)ᵀ = R(−θ)

equations.eq: RT = [R p; 0 1]
equations.note: Homogeneous transform: turn and move in one product; its columns are G's axes and origin in R

equations.eq: T⁻¹ = [Rᵀ −Rᵀp; 0 1]
equations.note: The way back; T⁻¹ is not Tᵀ
Frames in a chain multiply

practice.question: Frame G is turned 40° and its origin lies at (2, 3) in R. The point (5, 2) in G: what is its x in R?
The same point: its y in R?
Same frames; now the point (4, 8) is given in R. Its x in G?
practice.solution: Subtract the origin: (2, 5). Turn back by Rᵀ: x = 2 cos 40° + 5 sin 40° = 4.74; y = −2 sin 40° + 5 cos 40° = 2.54.

practice.question: And its y in G?
A frame moved by r = (2, 3), not turned; the point (1, 3) in it. Its y in the base frame?
A link l = 4 m at θ = 30°: the x of its tip?
practice.source: Worked by hand from ch. 2, p. 11 (the slide gives x = l cos θ)

practice.question: The way back: the tip at (4, 3) on a link l = 5 m. Its angle θ?
practice.source: Worked by hand from ch. 2, p. 11 (the slide gives θ = sin⁻¹(y/l))

labs.lecture: Ajanović (2020), ch. 2 Mathematische Beschreibung der Kinematik von Robotern, pp. 11–36

labs.title: Turning in space: Euler angles and gimbal lock
labs.idea: Three turns, each about an axis that the turns before have already moved, set any orientation. The order matters, the same matrix comes from more than one set of angles, and when the middle turn lines up the first and third axes one freedom is lost.

equations.eq: Rx(α) = [1 0 0; 0 cos α −sin α; 0 sin α cos α]
equations.note: Turn about x

equations.eq: Ry(β) = [cos β 0 sin β; 0 1 0; −sin β 0 cos β]
equations.note: Turn about y

equations.eq: Rz(γ) = [cos γ −sin γ 0; sin γ cos γ 0; 0 0 1]
equations.note: Turn about z

equations.eq: Rᵀ = R⁻¹, det R = 1
equations.note: A rotation matrix is orthonormal

equations.eq: ZY′X″ about moving axes = XYZ about fixed axes
equations.note: Turning about the fixed axes in the reverse order gives the same orientation

equations.eq: R = Rz(yaw) Ry(pitch) Rx(roll)
equations.note: Roll-pitch-yaw: roll about x, pitch about y, yaw about z, all fixed; the same as ZY′X″

equations.eq: X(α) Y(−90°) Z(γ) depends only on α + γ
equations.note: Gimbal lock: the first and third turns share one axis, a freedom is lost

practice.question: Z(0°) Y′(90°) X″(0°): the entry in row 3, column 1 of the rotation matrix?
practice.solution: Only Ry(90°) is left: its row 3 is (−sin 90°, 0, cos 90°) = (−1, 0, 0).

practice.question: Z(90°) Y′(90°) X″(90°): the entry in row 1, column 3?
practice.solution: The product is [0 0 1; 0 1 0; −1 0 0], the same matrix as Z(0°) Y′(90°) X″(0°): at Y′ = 90° the angles are not unique.

practice.question: Z(90°) Y′(90°) Z″(90°): the entry in row 1, column 1?
Z(90°) X′(−90°) Z″(−180°): the entry in row 2, column 1? (The slide finds these angles from the matrix.)
practice.source: Ajanović (2020), ch. 5, p. 8, printed (row 3 of the table)
practice.solution: The target is [0 0 −1; −1 0 0; 0 1 0]; row 2, column 1 is −1. Rows 1 and 2 of the slide's table (θ2 = 270°) give sin θ2 cos θ3 = 0, not 1, so they do not reach it.

labs.lecture: Ajanović (2020), ch. 2, pp. 39–61, and ch. 5, p. 8

labs.title: Where is the tip? Forward kinematics of a planar arm
labs.idea: Turn each joint and move along each link: multiplying one homogeneous transform per joint gives where the tip is and how it is turned. For every set of joint angles there is exactly one answer.
labs.law: x = l1 cos θ1 + l2 cos(θ1 + θ2), y = l1 sin θ1 + l2 sin(θ1 + θ2)
labs.lawTex: x = l_1\cos\theta_1 + l_2\cos(\theta_1+\theta_2),\quad y = l_1\sin\theta_1 + l_2\sin(\theta_1+\theta_2)

equations.eq: x = l1 cos θ1 + l2 cos(θ1 + θ2)
equations.note: Tip, x

equations.eq: y = l1 sin θ1 + l2 sin(θ1 + θ2)
equations.note: Tip, y

equations.eq: φ = θ1 + θ2
equations.note: The tip's turn

equations.eq: 0T2 = 0T1 · 1T2, iTj = [cos θ −sin θ l cos θ; sin θ cos θ l sin θ; 0 0 1]
equations.note: The same by transforms

equations.eq: x = k cos(α + θ1), y = l1 + k sin(α + θ1)
equations.tex: x = k\cos(\alpha+\theta_1),\quad y = l_1 + k\sin(\alpha+\theta_1),\quad k = \sqrt{(l_2 + l_3\cos 45^\circ)^2 + (l_4 + l_3\sin 45^\circ)^2}
equations.note: The bent arm: one turning joint, two fixed 135° bends

practice.question: The same arm: the tip's y?
practice.source: Ajanović (2020), ch. 2, p. 38, printed as 4.693 (4.6937 cut, not rounded)

practice.question: The same arm: the tip's turn φ?
practice.source: Worked by hand from ch. 2, p. 38
practice.solution: φ = θ1 + θ2 = 84°; cos 84° = 0.105 is the matrix's first entry.

practice.question: The bent arm, l1…l4 = 1, 2, 3, 4, at θ1 = 90°: the tip's x?
The bent arm at θ1 = 0°: the tip's y?

labs.lecture: Ajanović (2020), ch. 2, p. 38, and ch. 3 Vorwärtskinematik, pp. 2–3

labs.title: Four numbers per joint: the Denavit–Hartenberg chain
labs.idea: Put a frame on every link by four rules, and each step from one frame to the next needs only four numbers: θ, d, a and α. Multiply the steps and the chain gives the pose of its last frame.
labs.law: i−1Ti = Rot(z, θi) Trans(z, di) Trans(x, ai) Rot(x, αi)

equations.eq: zi along joint i + 1's axis; xi ⟂ zi−1 and meets zi−1; yi completes a right-handed frame
equations.note: The four DH rules for placing the frames

equations.eq: θi about zi−1, di along zi−1, ai along xi, αi about xi
equations.tex: \theta_i: x_{i-1}\to x_i \text{ about } z_{i-1},\; d_i \text{ along } z_{i-1},\; a_i \text{ along } x_i,\; \alpha_i: z_{i-1}\to z_i \text{ about } x_i
equations.note: The four parameters; θ is the variable of a turning joint, d of a sliding one

equations.eq: i−1Ti = [cθ −sθcα sθsα a cθ; sθ cθcα −cθsα a sθ; 0 sα cα d; 0 0 0 1]
equations.note: One DH step

equations.eq: 0Tn = 0T1 1T2 … n−1Tn
equations.note: The chain
The slides' RRT robot

practice.question: The RRT robot with l1…l4 = 1, 2, 3, 4 and l5* = 5, at θ1 = 0°, θ2 = 0°: the x of frame 3?
At θ1 = 0°, θ2 = 90°: the z of frame 3?
practice.solution: The arm points up: z = l1 + l2 + l4 + l5 = 12, x = l3 = 3.

practice.question: At θ1 = 90°, θ2 = 90°: the y of frame 3?
practice.solution: The first joint turns the offset l3 onto y: (0, 3, 12).

practice.question: At θ1 = 0°, θ2 = 0° with the stroke drawn in to l5* = 2: the x of frame 3?
practice.source: Worked by hand from ch. 3, p. 25 (the slide's ⁰T₃)
practice.solution: x = (l4 + l5) cos θ2 cos θ1 + l3 cos θ1 = 6 + 3 = 9.

labs.title: A real arm: the ABB IRB 120
labs.idea: The IRB 120's six axes as a DH chain built from the dimensions in its product specification. Set axes 2 and 3 to a row of the specification's working-range table and the chain puts the wrist centre where the table does.

equations.note: The DH table, built here from the dimensions in mm; checked against the working-range table
Base to axis 2, upper arm, step to the forearm, forearm, flange
Working ranges

equations.eq: J = [z × (p6 − pi−1); z] per turning joint
equations.note: The geometric Jacobian of the arm; det J = 0 where it loses a freedom, here when axis 5 is at 0°

practice.question: Axis 2 at 0°, axis 3 at −77°: the wrist centre's height Z?
practice.solution: The forearm stands upright: 290 + 270 + √(70² + 302²) = 290 + 270 + 310 = 870 mm; tan⁻¹(70/302) = 13° is why axis 3 must turn 77°, not 90°.

practice.question: Axis 2 at 0°, axis 3 at +70°: the wrist centre's reach X?
Axis 2 at +110°, axis 3 at −77°: the wrist centre's reach X?
practice.solution: Upper arm and forearm in line, 270 + 310 = 580 mm long, tilted 110° from upright: X = 580 sin 110° = 545 mm, Z = 290 + 580 cos 110° = 91 mm.

practice.question: Axis 2 at −110°, axis 3 at −110°: the wrist centre's height Z?
practice.solution: Elbow at (−253.7, 197.7) mm; the forearm turned a further −110° reaches 247.8 mm down: Z = −50 mm.

practice.question: Axis 2 at +90°, axis 3 at −77°: the wrist centre's reach X (the arm's 0.58 m reach)?
practice.source: ABB (2020), p. 31, row D, printed (its Z of 270 mm reads 290 mm by this chain)
practice.solution: Arm and forearm in line and level: X = 270 + 310 = 580 mm, at the shoulder's height of 290 mm.

labs.lecture: ABB (2020), IRB 120 product specification, pp. 11–12 and 31–32; Ajanović (2020), ch. 3, pp. 18–21, and ch. 4, p. 15

labs.title: How fast is the tip? The Jacobian and singular poses
labs.idea: The Jacobian turns joint speeds into the tip's speed. Its columns are what each joint alone does to the tip; where its determinant is zero the arm cannot move its tip one way at all, however fast the joints turn.

equations.eq: v = J(q) q̇, q̇ = J⁻¹(q) v
equations.note: Joint speeds to tip speed and back; the inverse exists only where det J ≠ 0

equations.tex: \mathbf{J}_v = \begin{pmatrix} \partial x/\partial q_1 & \cdots & \partial x/\partial q_n \\ \partial y/\partial q_1 & \cdots & \partial y/\partial q_n \\ \partial z/\partial q_1 & \cdots & \partial z/\partial q_n \end{pmatrix}
equations.note: The linear part by partial derivatives of the forward kinematics

equations.eq: Sliding joint: [z; 0]; turning joint: [z × (tn − ti−1); z]
equations.note: The geometric schema, from a DH chain

equations.eq: RT robot: ẋ = −(l1 + l2) sin θ1 θ̇1 + cos θ1 l̇2, ẏ = (l1 + l2) cos θ1 θ̇1 + sin θ1 l̇2, ωz = θ̇1
equations.note: A turning then a sliding joint
The planar two-link arm

equations.eq: det J = l1 l2 sin θ2
equations.note: Worked here from the matrix above: zero when the arm is stretched or folded

practice.question: The RT robot with l1 = 1, θ1 = 60°, stroke l2 = 2, turning at θ̇1 = 2 rad/s while the stroke grows at l̇2 = 0.5 per s: the tip's ẋ?
practice.source: Worked by hand from ch. 4, p. 18

practice.question: The same robot: the tip's ẏ?
practice.source: Worked by hand from ch. 4, p. 18

practice.question: The two-link arm l1 = 5, l2 = 3 at θ1 = 20°, θ2 = 64°: det J?
practice.source: Worked by hand from ch. 4, p. 20
practice.solution: det J = l1 l2 sin θ2 = 15 sin 64° = 13.48. It is largest, 15, at θ2 = ±90°, and zero at 0° and 180°.

labs.title: Which angles reach the target? Inverse kinematics of a two-link arm
labs.idea: Given the tip, find the joints. The two-link arm reaches a point in its ring of reach two ways, elbow one side or the other; on the ring's edge one way; outside it not at all. Obstacles and joint ranges decide which to take.
labs.law: cos θ2 = (x² + y² − l1² − l2²)/(2 l1 l2)

equations.tex: \theta_2 = \operatorname{atan2}\!\left(\pm\sqrt{1 - c_2^2},\; c_2\right),\quad c_2 = \frac{x^2 + y^2 - l_1^2 - l_2^2}{2\,l_1 l_2}
equations.note: Two elbow solutions

equations.eq: θ1 = atan2(y, x) − atan2(l2 sin θ2, l1 + l2 cos θ2)
equations.note: The shoulder for each elbow

equations.eq: (l1 − l2)² ≤ x² + y² ≤ (l1 + l2)²
equations.note: A solution exists only in the ring of reach

equations.eq: θ2 = 180° − arccos((c² − l1² − l2²)/(−2 l1 l2)), θ1 = arctan(y/x) − arccos((l2² − c² − l1²)/(−2 l1 c))
equations.tex: \theta_2 = 180^\circ - \arccos\frac{c^2 - l_1^2 - l_2^2}{-2 l_1 l_2},\quad \theta_1 = \arctan\frac{y}{x} - \arccos\frac{l_2^2 - c^2 - l_1^2}{-2 l_1 c}
equations.note: The same by the cosine rule in the triangle l1, l2, c = √(x² + y²)

equations.eq: θ1 = atan2(y, x), θ2 = atan2(z − l1, √(x² + y²))
equations.note: A post turning about its axis with a tilting arm on top: top view, then side view

practice.question: l1 = 3, l2 = 4, tip at (4, 3): θ1 of the solution with θ2 = +90°?
l1 = 5, l2 = 4, tip at (6, 5.93): the elbow angle θ2 of the positive solution?
The same: θ1 for θ2 = +41.05°?
l1 = 4, l2 = 1, tip at (2, 1): x² + y², to set against (l1 − l2)² = 9 and (l1 + l2)² = 25?
practice.source: Ajanović (2020), ch. 5, p. 19, printed: 9 ≤ 5 ≤ 25 fails, no solution
practice.solution: x² + y² = 4 + 1 = 5 < 9: the tip is inside the inner circle, which the arm cannot reach.

practice.question: The turning post of ch. 5, p. 21 with l1 = 2, l2 = 3 and the tip at (1.5, 2.598, 2): the turn θ1?
practice.source: Worked by hand from ch. 5, p. 21
practice.solution: θ1 = atan2(2.598, 1.5) = 60°; l2xy = 3, θ2 = atan2(0, 3) = 0°: the arm lies level.

labs.title: Exercise: the RRT robot by DH, step by step
labs.idea: The slides' RRT robot solved as on the slides: fill the DH table one row at a time while each frame appears on the arm, then multiply the three steps into the pose entry by entry and set it beside the three poses the slide prints. Each step shows its Python and MATLAB.

equations.eq: ⁱ⁻¹Tᵢ = Rot(z, θᵢ) Trans(z, dᵢ) Trans(x, aᵢ) Rot(x, αᵢ)
equations.note: One DH step, the matrix each row of the table gives
The RRT robot's DH table

equations.eq: ⁰T₃ = ⁰T₁ · ¹T₂ · ²T₃
equations.note: The pose of the TCP: the steps multiplied in order

practice.question: The RRT robot (l1…l4 = 1…4, l5* = 5) at θ1 = 0°, θ2 = 90°: the x of the TCP?
At θ1 = 90°, θ2 = 0° (not printed): the y of the TCP?
practice.source: Worked by hand from ch. 3, p. 25 (the slide's ⁰T₃)

labs.title: Exercise: the IRB 120 at the student's joint values
labs.idea: The student's own DH table of the IRB 120, seven rows from the project report, beside this lab's six; both multiplied into the flange's pose and set against the student's printed home pose and every row of the specification's working-range table. Each step shows its Python and MATLAB.

equations.eq: ⁰T₆ = ⁰T₁ ¹T₂ ⋯ ⁵T₆
equations.note: The flange's pose, the DH steps multiplied in order
This lab's DH table, built from the dimensions; θ2 has a −90° offset

equations.eq: wrist centre = flange − 72 mm along its z
equations.note: The point the working-range table gives

practice.question: The IRB 120 with every axis at 0°: the flange's x?
practice.solution: Wrist centre at 302 mm (ABB p. 31, row A) plus the 72 mm flange along x: 374 mm, at a height of 630 mm.

practice.question: The same pose with axis 5 at 90°: the flange's height z?
practice.source: Worked by hand from ABB p. 12
practice.solution: Axis 5 tips the flange down: z = 630 − 72 = 558 mm, x = 302 mm.

labs.lecture: ABB (2020), pp. 12 and 31; the student's forward_kinematics(spyder).py and report

labs.title: Exercise: the Jacobian column by column, then its singularity
labs.idea: Build the two-link arm's Jacobian by the course's schema: each column is the joint's axis crossed with the lever arm to the tip. Then close the elbow and watch det J fall to zero as the two columns line up. Each step shows its Python and MATLAB.

equations.eq: Jᵢ = z_{i−1} × (p − p_{i−1}) for a turning joint
equations.note: The schema's column of a turning joint

equations.tex: J = \begin{pmatrix} -l_1 s_1 - l_2 s_{12} & -l_2 s_{12} \\ l_1 c_1 + l_2 c_{12} & l_2 c_{12} \end{pmatrix}
equations.note: The two-link arm's position rows

equations.eq: det J = l1 l2 sin θ2
equations.note: Zero when the arm is stretched or folded

practice.question: l1 = 5, l2 = 3, θ1 = 20°, θ2 = 10°: det J?
practice.source: Worked by hand from ch. 4, p. 20
practice.solution: det J = 15 sin 10° = 2.605: a fifth of its value at 64°, the arm near stretched.

practice.question: The same arm stretched, θ2 = 0°: det J?
practice.source: Worked by hand from ch. 4, p. 20
practice.solution: sin 0° = 0: both columns point the same way, across the arm.

labs.title: Exercise: elbow up and down, then the IRB 120's wrist split
labs.idea: Solve the slides' two-link arm both ways, back a three-link arm off to its wrist, then split the IRB 120 the same way: the wrist centre sets axes 1–3, what is left of the turn sets axes 4–6. Each step shows its Python and MATLAB.
labs.law: cos θ2 = (x² + y² − l1² − l2²)/(2 l1 l2)

equations.eq: θ2 = atan2(±√(1 − c2²), c2), θ1 = atan2(y, x) − atan2(l2 sin θ2, l1 + l2 cos θ2)
equations.note: Both elbows of the two-link arm

equations.eq: wrist = TCP − l3 (cos φ, sin φ), θ3 = φ − θ1 − θ2
equations.note: The three-link arm split at its wrist

equations.eq: w = p − 72 z₆, q1 = atan2(wy, wx); ³R₆ = ⁰R₃ᵀ R = Rz(q4) Ry(−q5) Rz(q6)
equations.note: The IRB 120's wrist split, for this lab's DH table

practice.question: l1 = 5, l2 = 4, TCP (6 | 5.93): θ1 of the solution with θ2 = −41.05°?
Three-link arm l1 = 3, l2 = 4, l3 = 2, TCP (4, 3), tool angle φ = 30°: θ3 of the solution with θ2 > 0?
practice.source: Worked by hand from ch. 5, pp. 17–18

practice.question: The IRB 120's flange at axes (30°, 20°, 10°, 0°, 45°, 0°): axis 2 back from the wrist split, the elbow whose triangle angle is negative?
practice.source: By definition: forward, then back, gives the axes again
practice.solution: w = flange − 72 z₆; q1 = atan2(wy, wx) = 30°; the arm's triangle of 270 mm and 310 mm gives q2 = 20°, q3 = 10° (the other elbow: 114.43°, −163.90°, outside axis 3's range).
